newsitem.title: USA: California drives western US econ growth--S.F. Fed.
newsitem.headline: California drives western US econ growth--S.F. Fed.

text.p: The California economy is exuberant, spurred by a booming high-technology industry and blossoming manufacturing and service businesses, an official at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco said.
"California continues to improve. At this point, it is growing at a very strong pace for such a large economy," Robert Valletta, regional economist at the San Francisco Fed, told Reuters.
Like the old days when thousands flocked to California in search of gold and wealth, the now "Silicon State" has once again been the main engine driving the western U.S. economy.

"Because the Californian economy has been growing at a good clip and its labor market has been tightening, we see further tightening for the (12th economic) district as a whole," the San Francisco Fed economist said.
Unlike the national average indicators, which suggest an incipient but steady economic slowdown, the economy of the 12th district is showing no signs of emerging weakness.
"We are not really seeing a noticeable slowdown. In fact we're experiencing exactly the opposite ... We don't see any slackening in the district at this point," Valletta said.
The nation's 12th economic district includes Alaska, Arizona, California, Hawaii, Nevada, Idaho, Utah and Washington, plus Guam, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands.

It is the largest economic district in the nation, with 1.3 million square miles, or 35 percent of the country's area. It ranks second in the Federal Reserve System in terms of deposits held by large commercial banks.
In a more detailed analysis of the region's economy, Valletta said some states in the region -- notably Nevada, Utah and Idaho -- have showed some signs of a slowdown.
The San Francisco Fed economist added, however, that those economies were not stepping on the brakes, but rather taking their foot off the gas.
"The thing to keep in mind is that, particularly with Nevada and Utah, they've been growing so rapidly that a slight slowdown is hardly even worth paying attention to," he said.
Valletta said the Washington economy also remains healthy, bolstered mainly by stunning performances by aircraft and software behemoths Boeing and Microsoft.
The only state in the region bucking the trend is Hawaii.
"It's just Hawaii that is still not doing real well. Employment is still declining there," Valletta said.
The 12th district expansion, however, has shown some singularities.
Despite the strong growth currently seen in California, the state's unemployment rate remains at 6.5 percent, well above the 4.8 percent average for the nation.
Valletta also said no significant increases in wages and prices have been perceived by the San Francisco Fed.

"We don't see any noticeable uptick in wage and price pressures. So to the extent those pressures might be building, they have not manifested themselves yet," he said. Valletta added that it was hard to predict when or if such a phenomenon would occur.
The San Francisco Fed economist said the district's economy was sound, refuting the idea that the region's turnaround was volatile because it was too dependent on the high-technology industry.
"A lot of the growth in the California economy has been stimulated by the tremendous success of the computer sector.
"But on the other hand that sector in and on itself is quite diversified ... It's not that we have all our eggs in one basket," the Fed economist said.

Valletta also said many jobs in the region have been created in more traditional manufacturing industries, such as textiles, and in the services sector, which provided a solid foundation for the current expansion.
